title: Teaching Is Absurd
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. uses October's reputation as the month teachers hit the Wall to examine the four structural absurdities that make teaching genuinely crazy: the finitude of the teacher, the boundless complexity of each student, the timeless depth of the disciplines being taught, and the dystopian contemporary context in which all this unfolds. He argues that these absurdities are not problems to be solved but realities to be named, laughed at, and embraced — positioning teaching alongside other historically significant human endeavors that also contained absurd ingredients. Rather than treating the scale of the work as a reason for despair, Stuart Jr. argues it is a reason for earnestness and craft: massive good comes from regular classrooms led by regular teachers doing awake, purposeful work, and that good ripples for generations even when the teacher never knows its extent.
points: October is 'Special Opportunity Month' — the month teachers hit the Wall; naming this difficulty as a predictable, structural feature of the teaching year rather than a personal failure is itself a form of struggle normalization.
The four absurdities of teaching — teacher finitude, student complexity, disciplinary depth, dystopian context — are not problems to be solved but tensions to be held with humor and earnest craft.

Laughter is a professional tool: if the absurdity of the work does not produce humor, it will produce despair, and experienced teachers learn that choosing humor is both more accurate and more sustaining.
Despite the four absurdities, massive good will come from earnest, craft-conscious teaching; the right standard is not perfection but being awake — present, attentive, committed to the work.
Simple, good work in a classroom produces good that ripples for generations, even when — especially when — the teacher never knows the full downstream impact of what they did.
quotes: We are constrained beings, limited in our time and energy and inability to multitask. Despite the ethos of our times, we can't do it all, be it all, complete it all, achieve it all. No amount of machinery or technology will ever change that either.

Each of them is a never-before-seen instance of humanity, fearfully and wonderfully wrought. They are mostly invisible creatures — we can see their faces and their work but not the immense web of experiences and relationships and chemicals and hormones and beliefs that make them them.
Teaching is absurd in that it entails us finite creatures working to connect dozens of boundlessly complex students with the cosmos-depths of disciplines in a rather dystopian context.

Because despite these absurdities, a massive good will come from our work this year, provided that we pursue it with the earnestness and craftsmanship and spirit our profession calls for. I'm not talking about doing it perfectly; I'm talking about doing it awake.

Good comes from regular classrooms led by regular teachers like you and me, even in the midst of the wildness of what we're doing. We really never know what good our work will do, but at the same time we can be confident that simple, good work in a classroom will do a kind of good that ripples on for generations.
